title: Peter and Paul in Rome (c. 64–67)
hook: tradition holds Peter was crucified upside down and Paul beheaded under Nero

segments.voice: Yesterday, church history: Acts stops in Rome, and the long record begins. Your line was saints and sinners, both.

By the Sea of Tiberias, after a breakfast of bread and fish, the risen Jesus tells Peter how his life will end. When you were younger, he says, you dressed yourself and walked where you liked. When you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and lead you where you would not go. John adds one quiet line: this was to show by what death Peter would glorify God. Then the Bible goes silent. Where Peter's road ends, and Paul's, is told by the generations after.
screen: `BY THE SEA OF TIBERIAS.` → `YOU WILL STRETCH OUT YOUR HANDS.` → `THE BIBLE GOES SILENT.`

segments.voice: Start with Paul. In the Second Letter to Timothy, Paul writes as a prisoner to a younger friend, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." A few lines later he asks Timothy to hurry before winter, and bring the cloak he left behind, and his books. A man who knows the end is close. Now the tradition. Early Christian writers, collected by the historian Eusebius, say both apostles died in Rome under the emperor Nero. Tradition says Paul, a Roman citizen as Acts tells us, was beheaded. And it says Peter was crucified, and asked to hang head downward, because he did not think himself worthy to die the way his Lord had. That detail comes from writings outside the Bible; Catholics hold it as tradition, not scripture. Now the names. In Matthew's Gospel Jesus gives Simon a new one: "thou art Peter; and upon this rock I will build my church." Catholics see the bishops of Rome as Peter's successors, and Saint Peter's Basilica stands over the place tradition names as his grave. The tentmaker: Acts says Paul made tents with his hands, and Paul writes that he labored night and day so as not to be a burden. A fisherman and a craftsman, and not always at peace: Paul says he opposed Peter to his face in Antioch over who could eat with whom. Yet the Church keeps their feast together, on one day. Some paintings set them side by side, Peter with the keys, Paul with the sword that tradition says took his head, and between them a quarrel neither the Bible nor the Church ever hid.
screen: `I HAVE KEPT THE FAITH.` · `ROME, UNDER NERO: TRADITION.` · `THE ROCK AND THE TENTMAKER.` · `TWO WHO ARGUED, ONE FEAST.` · then, large: `UPON THIS ROCK I WILL BUILD MY CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Remember Christians who suffer for their faith today. You don't need names: just someone, somewhere, who will go to Mass this week knowing it could cost them a job, a home, their safety. If you pray, ask for their courage and protection, and for the people who threaten them; if you don't, keep them in mind.
Cephas. The Aramaic name John also gives Simon Peter, alongside the Greek Petros, rock. Today's word.
Your line: the rock and the tentmaker. Two very different men, one feast. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics keep one shared feast for Saints Peter and Paul, pray at the tombs tradition names as theirs in Rome, and pray for persecuted Christians at Mass and in their own prayers.

chat.says: Does the Bible say Peter was crucified upside down in Rome?
options: No. John hints at how he'd die; Rome and the upside-down cross come from tradition.
Yes, Acts ends by describing how both Peter and Paul died in Rome under Nero.
Yes, Paul tells the story in his letter to Timothy, written just after Peter died.
chat.meaning: The Bible goes silent on their deaths. Early writers gathered by Eusebius say both died in Rome under Nero; the cross head downward is tradition.

Tiberias.meaning: the lake in Galilee, as John's Gospel names it

Eusebius.meaning: an early historian who collected writings about the Church

Antioch.meaning: the city where Paul opposed Peter to his face

Cephas.meaning: Aramaic for rock, a name John gives Simon Peter

Petros.meaning: Greek for rock, the name Peter

notes: 2 Timothy 4:7 and Matthew 16:18 Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording: confirm exact text.
Script attributes the Nero-era deaths in Rome to tradition via Eusebius (HE 2.25 citing Gaius and Dionysius of Corinth; HE 3.1 citing Origen for Peter crucified head downward). Confirm references.

Peter's reason (unworthy to die as the Lord did) follows the Acts of Peter and later tradition (e.g. Jerome); Origen via Eusebius gives head downward without that reason in some readings. Confirm attribution.
Pauline authorship of 2 Timothy is debated by some scholars; script calls it 'the second letter to Timothy' and does not argue the point.
Title date 'c. 64–67' is the index's; script states no date in the voice.
Shared feast of Peter and Paul (29 June) mentioned without date.

Audit: the teach ended by saying the Church keeps them together twice in a row; the close now ends on the keys, the sword and the quarrel nobody hid. The sword as the instrument of Paul's death is iconographic tradition: confirm.
